# Repository Guidelines

## Project decisions

Consult the [decision log](docs/decisions.md) when a task touches a prior design
choice or revisits a recurring question. Add or update a concise entry when
discussion, implementation or verification settles something that will affect
future work.

## Reliability before implementation

- For new events, subscriptions, timers and polling changes, consult the
  [event-driven design guide](docs/event-driven-design.md) and
  [scheduled work guide](docs/scheduled-work.md) before editing.

- For background work, synchronization, storage, caching or UI-state changes, read
  [performance requirements](docs/performance-requirements.md). Identify the work
  trigger, resource budget, accumulation/reclamation policy and applicable
  performance regression before editing; record measured limits and remaining
  gaps. Apply its [startup, idle and active-business checklist](docs/performance-requirements.md#apply-to-every-feature)
  to every affected phase, including return to idle after use. Extend its general
  rules when a confirmed defect reveals a new pattern.
  Apply the [headless post-office checklist](docs/performance-requirements.md#headless-post-office-nodes)
  to relay changes and register background work with the
  [existing event or scheduling owner](docs/event-driven-design.md#register-relay-work-with-its-owner).

- Before implementing, refactoring, fixing or reviewing code, read the
  [AI coding reliability guide](docs/ai-coding-reliability.md), select the rules
  triggered by the changed boundaries, and inspect the owning code and callers.
  For concurrency/lifecycle changes, trace lock order, wait dependencies, actual
  work ownership, cancellation and commit authority before editing.
- Validate the applicable failure and recovery paths, not only the happy path.
  Record concrete evidence and remaining limits; a timeout, successful build or
  passing subset is not proof that UI freezes or all deadlocks are impossible.
- When a confirmed defect exposes a reusable failure pattern, update that guide's
  existing rule or add a distinct rule with its owner and regression evidence.
  Maintain the owning contract and test selectors; keep incident logs out of the guide.

## Project Structure & Module Organization

- Four-crate Rust workspace. `crates/mesh-talk-core/` is the UI-free protocol core (lib
  `mesh_talk_core` + the `mesh-talk-node` CLI bin in `src/bin/`): feature modules `node/`,
  `identity/`, `transport/`, `discovery/`, `eventlog/`, `ratchet/`, `channel/`, `dm.rs`,
  `file/`, `postoffice/`, `storage/`. `src-tauri/` is the Tauri desktop app: entry
  `src/main.rs` → `lib.rs`, IPC glue in `commands.rs` (auth) + `chat_commands/` (messaging)
  - `events.rs`, plus `state.rs`, `tray.rs`, `services/` (auth only).
- `crates/mesh-talk-integrations/` owns scoped local messaging grants, private IPC,
  and the dedicated bot host/admin CLI; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp/` adapts its four
  send/context/status tools to the official MCP SDK. Neither owns mesh crypto.
- Integration/e2e suites live in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` (`two_node_cli`,
  `persistent_history`, `post_office_offline`, `decoder_smoke`); keep unit tests inline via
  `mod tests` (e.g. `node/node_tests.rs`).
- React client sits in `frontend/src`; Vite tooling in `frontend/package.json`.
- Operational scripts in `scripts/` (`setup-hooks.sh`, `check-health.sh`); architecture in
  `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`; conventions in `specifications/`. The
  [documentation map](docs/README.md) routes readers to maintained guides; the
  [documentation guidelines](docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md) define ownership
  across the README, guides, and project site.

## Build, Test, and Development Commands

- `make dev` primes Rust + Node deps and installs git hooks.
- `make build` / `make frontend-build` — release build / Vite production build.
- During feature development, preview changed-boundary validation with `make test-plan`
  and run it with `make test-changed`. Unmapped changes require an explicit owner
  and reason; inspect escalation notes for browser/native or consumer checks.
  Use `make verify-plan` / `make verify-changed` at task completion to compose the
  same affected tests with applicable formatting, lint/types and builds. The
  test-only commands do not include static checks; neither mode replaces required
  PR/review, browser/native or release gates. `make validation-report` separates
  queue and execution costs; `make validation-audit` compares a clean affected
  plan with same-source broader failure evidence before narrowing any gate.
  Read selected capability references and inspect pending browser/native requirements.
  Execution prints a structured feedback report; follow the
  [validation protocol](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#validation-stages-and-agent-responsibilities)
  for completed work, remaining evidence and additive semantic selections.
- During feature development, run affected tests only: `make test-focused
TEST_PACKAGE=mesh-talk-core TEST_FILTER=node::account_sync` selects Rust unit
  tests; add `TEST_TARGET=bridge_cross_lan` to select one integration target.
  `cd frontend && npm test -- src/features/chat/settingsDialogSession.test.ts`
  selects a frontend unit file. `make test` runs the full workspace suite
  (`cargo test --workspace`) for pre-PR and CI gates;
  `make e2e` runs the `#[ignore]`d multi-process backend rigs; `cd frontend && npm run e2e`
  runs the Playwright UI suite. Test builds use cheap KDF params (the `fast-test-kdf`
  feature), and `.cargo/config.toml` caps test/compile parallelism.
- UI / node spot checks: `make tauri-dev`, `make frontend-dev`,
  `cargo run -p mesh-talk-core --bin mesh-talk-node -- --keystore /tmp/a.keystore
--password pw --name alice` (add `--post-office` for relay mode).

## Coding Style & Naming Conventions

- Rust: `cargo fmt` (4-space, `snake_case` modules, `UpperCamelCase` types) +
  **`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`** (must match CI — `--all-targets` covers
  tests/benches).
- Frontend: `npm run format` (Prettier) + `npm run lint` (ESLint flat config).
- Write documentation and reusable prompts in English unless a specific exception is needed.
- Reference `specifications/development_conventions.md` for naming nuances.

## Domain Language

- `CONTEXT.md` is the canonical domain glossary. `docs/domain-design.md` indexes
  the modeling references and defines DDD vocabulary and naming translations.
- Distinguish local users, accounts and devices; desktop, transport and ratchet
  sessions; discovery, presence, custody, recipient delivery and read state.
- Use explicit identity/lifetime names in new code. Preserve public, wire and
  stored identifiers unless a separately validated compatibility change is intended.
- Update the glossary and affected owning guides when a domain meaning changes;
  link to definitions instead of maintaining duplicate glossaries.

## Architecture & Components

- Before adding business logic, consult [module ownership and reuse](docs/module-boundaries.md),
  inspect the owning module and its callers, and extend its existing implementation.
  Parallel tasks should name their owned paths and shared-interface dependencies;
  coordinate changes to shared interfaces through one integration owner. Keep
  feature-specific helpers local and share rules when their meaning and lifecycle
  are the same. The guide owns the detailed assignment and handoff contract.
- Stack: Rust 2024 on Tokio; Tauri 2 + React shell. No vendor-operated server.
- The `Node` (`node/node.rs`) wires identity + signed UDP **multicast** discovery
  (group `224.0.0.167`, port 47474) + Noise-encrypted TCP transport (`transport/`,
  low-level socket in `transport/net.rs`) + the content-addressed event log + DM/channel/
  file crypto. Messages are events synced as a bounded append-only log, account-addressed
  across a user's devices; optional offline custody via equal eligible post offices.
  Routed discovery and opt-in post-office federation connect reachable sites without
  joining their IP subnets. Wire formats are versioned bincode.
- See **`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`** before changing crypto, sync, or transport;
  **`docs/network-design-reference.md`** owns the communication invariants,
  module contracts, resource budgets and topology acceptance boundaries.

## Maintaining standards as requirements change

- When changing production dependencies, bundled assets, compiler profiles or
  installer settings, check [package size budgets](docs/updates.md#manual-package-size-budgets).
  Compare download bytes against a baseline for the same platform, architecture
  and installer format. Record installed footprint separately and explain each
  meaningful increase. If a production package was unavailable, record that
  evidence gap. Preserve native install, update and signature verification.

- Before changing tests, fixtures, dependencies or workflows in ways that affect
  CI cost or reliability, read [CI maintenance](docs/ci-maintenance.md). Reuse
  existing owners, measure the affected cost, and preserve acceptance evidence;
  keep required-check policy in its existing owner.
- Before implementation, identify the existing decision owner, authoritative rule,
  observable acceptance criteria, affected consumers and required boundary evidence.
  Extend the owning implementation and `validation.json`; new business capabilities
  should link their guide and invariants. Explain an unchanged contract in the PR.
- Run `make standards-check` after adding/moving source or changing contracts. It
  checks structural ownership and maintained references, including new files; it
  does not prove assertion quality, semantic completeness or candidate readiness.
  Hooks inspect the working tree, so partially staged commits still need a clean
  committed-candidate check in CI. Frontend dependencies must be installed.
- When CI exposes a local omission or flaky fixture, fix the owning selector, task
  or fixture and add a focused regression. Review timing and selection evidence
  before changing policy. Follow the maintained
  [requirement maintenance loop](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#maintaining-standards-across-requirements).

## Testing Guidelines

- Integration coverage in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` and `node/node_tests.rs`; embed
  unit tests near the code. Networking/crypto changes ship a loopback integration assertion.
- Backend multi-process E2E via `make e2e` (CI: `e2e-backend.yml`); Playwright UI E2E via
  `cd frontend && npm run e2e` (CI: `e2e-ui.yml`).
- Do not run full suites or E2E automatically during ordinary feature work. Run
  the affected unit or integration tests as changes are made; run E2E and the
  comprehensive health gate on explicit request, for optional full local preparation,
  or in CI.
- See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for selection examples and escalation triggers.
- Document executed validation commands in every PR; ensure `make test` passes
  locally or through its matching CI workspace suite before merge.

## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines

- Before changing product versions or release automation, read [the version lifecycle](docs/updates.md#version-ownership-and-lifecycle).
  Root `Cargo.toml` `[workspace.package].version` is authoritative. Use
  `node scripts/release/version.mjs check|sync|prepare VERSION` (the `VERSION` argument belongs
  to `prepare` only); do not hand-edit generated npm/Cargo lock metadata or introduce another
  version constant. Root private npm metadata is a checked release-tooling projection;
  frontend private metadata is versionless and Tauri inherits Cargo. Never broadly replace
  matching dependency, fixture, history, wire or schema versions. Keep source builds `BASE-dev`,
  Nightlies `BASE-nightly.RUN.ATTEMPT`, official tagged builds `BASE`, and standard SemVer ordering.
- Version/changelog preparation and next-development-target changes use reviewed PRs. Ordinary main
  pushes must not create automatic release proposals or commit-derived product notes. Stable publication
  remains explicit through the existing verified tagged-release workflow; no direct main push,
  public empty release, mutable published tag or gate bypass. Nightly publication requires trusted
  `main` and a target above the latest Stable. Future changes must extend the existing version
  owner, its tests, standards/CI enforcement and capability contracts together; the owning guide
  documents permissions, bot-PR checks, dispatch and recovery requirements. Manual Stable draft
  preparation uses the reviewed exact-version CHANGELOG section and requires exact-source checks
  before creating its immutable tag/draft. The fixed release-history
  migration floor is historical provenance; never advance it during ordinary version bumps.

- Conventional commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`); scopes like `feat(node):` align with
  `specifications/git_standards.md`. Squash WIP; link issues. When asked to merge,
  default to squash merge unless the user explicitly requests another strategy;
  follow the [merge policy](specifications/git_standards.md#pull-request-merge-strategy)
  and current-head required checks.
- Create PRs through `./scripts/create-pr.sh -- <gh pr create options>`.
  The default checks the clean committed candidate, comparison base, argument safety,
  whitespace, cheap affected static checks, ownership blockers, structural standards,
  repository hygiene and applicable verified frontend patch coverage before publication.
  Use `make pr-check` for the same cheap static phase; missing current coverage
  evidence reports its explicit generation command and never starts suites implicitly.
  CI runs after publication; full-scope candidates retain cross-platform execution.
  Only the proven [documentation scope](docs/ci-maintenance.md#documentation-only-pr-scope)
  may omit unrelated product tests. All required checks must pass on the current PR head before merging. Creating a PR does not certify test acceptance.
- To run comprehensive checks locally before publication, use
  `./scripts/create-pr.sh --full-preflight <selectors/specs> -- <gh pr create options>`.
  This invokes `prepare-pr.sh` (platform preflight plus full health). For an existing
  PR, `./scripts/prepare-pr.sh <selectors/specs>` provides the same optional local gate.
  Use Playwright specs relevant to changed frontend behavior and repeated
  `--core-filter` / `--host-filter` / `--integration-filter` / `--mcp-filter` selectors
  for changed Rust crates. Preflight runs selected tests in Linux Docker and through
  SSH to `windows10`; Windows workspaces, caches and temporary data stay on drive D.
  Owning scenario rules add visual specs and require real native evidence for
  lifecycle/discovery changes. Missing environments or empty Rust selections fail
  full preflight. Include `e2e/ui-visual-regression.spec.ts` for theme/layout changes.
  See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for configuration, coverage and plan preview.
  Fetch `origin/main` first if the comparison base is stale.
- Record focused validation and outstanding checks in the PR. Use
  `./scripts/check-health.sh` when comprehensive local evidence is needed; protected
  CI remains required before merge regardless of local results.

## Security & Adjustments

- `./scripts/check-health.sh` chains fmt, Clippy `--all-targets`, ESLint, tests, typos,
  cargo-deny, cargo-machete, gitleaks, shellcheck, audits, and both builds.
- Triage vulnerabilities immediately or document mitigation in the PR.
- If plans shift, update the relevant committed design or architecture docs. Keep
  `docs/superpowers/` and the root `plans/` directory local and untracked.

## Repository Hygiene

### Worktree lifecycle

- Create a worktree only when isolation is needed. Before creating one, inspect
  `git worktree list --porcelain` and record the task-owned path, branch and any
  dedicated build directory in ignored `tmp/` task notes. Treat pre-existing
  worktrees and unrelated changes as user-owned; never sweep them automatically.
- The coordinating session owns cleanup of every worktree it creates or delegates,
  including `.worktrees/` and `.claude/worktrees/agent-*`. Delegate completion does
  not transfer that responsibility. Before ending the task, stop task-owned
  processes and remove its worktrees, disposable branches and dedicated Cargo
  target directories, subject to the preservation rules below. Never delete a
  shared target directory or a directory whose ownership is uncertain.
- Before removal, preserve the work through either a verified merge into the
  intended integration branch under the existing PR/merge gates, or a local
  archive. For an archive, commit only task-owned outstanding changes (including
  intended untracked files), run the required commit checks, and create a unique
  `archive/<worktree-name>-<timestamp>` tag at the final branch tip. Verify the tag
  resolves to that tip and the worktree is clean before deleting anything. Never
  overwrite an existing archive tag, include secrets/ignored build output, or
  discard unrelated edits to make cleanup succeed. Cleanup does not authorize
  merging, pushing, bypassing review or running `entire clean`.
- Run removal from a surviving checkout with `git worktree remove <path>`, then
  `git branch -d <branch>` for a merged branch. Use `git branch -D <branch>` only
  for a task-owned archived branch after verifying its archive tag. Never use
  forced worktree removal, hard reset or bulk directory deletion to bypass a
  dirty worktree. Detached worktrees require the same preservation of their final
  commit before removal; there is no branch to delete.
- A pending PR, unresolved conflict, user decision, active concurrent session or
  failed preservation/cleanup step is an explicit retention exception. Preserve
  the required branch for an open PR; remove its clean worktree if no active work
  needs it. Recheck `git worktree list --porcelain` and task-owned branches/build
  paths before the final reply. Report cleanup performed and name every retained
  path/branch, its reason and the next action; never silently leave task worktrees.

- Keep implementation plans, research, investigation notes and scratch scripts
  under ignored `tmp/`; remove them when the work is complete.
- Merge durable decisions into the maintained owning guide. Do not commit
  completed-work reports, score histories, duplicate runbooks or archive copies.
- `docs/evals/` owns reusable suites/inventories, prompts and its README only.
  Generated evidence belongs in ignored output or PR/CI artifacts.
- Run `node scripts/check-repository-hygiene.mjs` before committing. The shared
  index check also runs in pre-commit, CI and health, rejecting ignored files
  even when force-added. See `docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md` for ownership.

</INSTRUCTIONS>

# Repository Guidelines

## Project decisions

Consult the [decision log](docs/decisions.md) when a task touches a prior design
choice or revisits a recurring question. Add or update a concise entry when
discussion, implementation or verification settles something that will affect
future work.

## Reliability before implementation

- For new events, subscriptions, timers and polling changes, consult the
  [event-driven design guide](docs/event-driven-design.md) and
  [scheduled work guide](docs/scheduled-work.md) before editing.

- For background work, synchronization, storage, caching or UI-state changes, read
  [performance requirements](docs/performance-requirements.md). Identify the work
  trigger, resource budget, accumulation/reclamation policy and applicable
  performance regression before editing; record measured limits and remaining
  gaps. Apply its [startup, idle and active-business checklist](docs/performance-requirements.md#apply-to-every-feature)
  to every affected phase, including return to idle after use. Extend its general
  rules when a confirmed defect reveals a new pattern.
  Apply the [headless post-office checklist](docs/performance-requirements.md#headless-post-office-nodes)
  to relay changes and register background work with the
  [existing event or scheduling owner](docs/event-driven-design.md#register-relay-work-with-its-owner).

- Before implementing, refactoring, fixing or reviewing code, read the
  [AI coding reliability guide](docs/ai-coding-reliability.md), select the rules
  triggered by the changed boundaries, and inspect the owning code and callers.
  For concurrency/lifecycle changes, trace lock order, wait dependencies, actual
  work ownership, cancellation and commit authority before editing.
- Validate the applicable failure and recovery paths, not only the happy path.
  Record concrete evidence and remaining limits; a timeout, successful build or
  passing subset is not proof that UI freezes or all deadlocks are impossible.
- When a confirmed defect exposes a reusable failure pattern, update that guide's
  existing rule or add a distinct rule with its owner and regression evidence.
  Maintain the owning contract and test selectors; keep incident logs out of the guide.

## Project Structure & Module Organization

- Four-crate Rust workspace. `crates/mesh-talk-core/` is the UI-free protocol core (lib
  `mesh_talk_core` + the `mesh-talk-node` CLI bin in `src/bin/`): feature modules `node/`,
  `identity/`, `transport/`, `discovery/`, `eventlog/`, `ratchet/`, `channel/`, `dm.rs`,
  `file/`, `postoffice/`, `storage/`. `src-tauri/` is the Tauri desktop app: entry
  `src/main.rs` → `lib.rs`, IPC glue in `commands.rs` (auth) + `chat_commands/` (messaging)
  - `events.rs`, plus `state.rs`, `tray.rs`, `services/` (auth only).
- `crates/mesh-talk-integrations/` owns scoped local messaging grants, private IPC,
  and the dedicated bot host/admin CLI; `crates/mesh-talk-mcp/` adapts its four
  send/context/status tools to the official MCP SDK. Neither owns mesh crypto.
- Integration/e2e suites live in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` (`two_node_cli`,
  `persistent_history`, `post_office_offline`, `decoder_smoke`); keep unit tests inline via
  `mod tests` (e.g. `node/node_tests.rs`).
- React client sits in `frontend/src`; Vite tooling in `frontend/package.json`.
- Operational scripts in `scripts/` (`setup-hooks.sh`, `check-health.sh`); architecture in
  `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`; conventions in `specifications/`. The
  [documentation map](docs/README.md) routes readers to maintained guides; the
  [documentation guidelines](docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md) define ownership
  across the README, guides, and project site.

## Build, Test, and Development Commands

- `make dev` primes Rust + Node deps and installs git hooks.
- `make build` / `make frontend-build` — release build / Vite production build.
- During feature development, preview changed-boundary validation with `make test-plan`
  and run it with `make test-changed`. Unmapped changes require an explicit owner
  and reason; inspect escalation notes for browser/native or consumer checks.
  Use `make verify-plan` / `make verify-changed` at task completion to compose the
  same affected tests with applicable formatting, lint/types and builds. The
  test-only commands do not include static checks; neither mode replaces required
  PR/review, browser/native or release gates. `make validation-report` separates
  queue and execution costs; `make validation-audit` compares a clean affected
  plan with same-source broader failure evidence before narrowing any gate.
  Read selected capability references and inspect pending browser/native requirements.
  Execution prints a structured feedback report; follow the
  [validation protocol](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#validation-stages-and-agent-responsibilities)
  for completed work, remaining evidence and additive semantic selections.
- During feature development, run affected tests only: `make test-focused
TEST_PACKAGE=mesh-talk-core TEST_FILTER=node::account_sync` selects Rust unit
  tests; add `TEST_TARGET=bridge_cross_lan` to select one integration target.
  `cd frontend && npm test -- src/features/chat/settingsDialogSession.test.ts`
  selects a frontend unit file. `make test` runs the full workspace suite
  (`cargo test --workspace`) for pre-PR and CI gates;
  `make e2e` runs the `#[ignore]`d multi-process backend rigs; `cd frontend && npm run e2e`
  runs the Playwright UI suite. Test builds use cheap KDF params (the `fast-test-kdf`
  feature), and `.cargo/config.toml` caps test/compile parallelism.
- UI / node spot checks: `make tauri-dev`, `make frontend-dev`,
  `cargo run -p mesh-talk-core --bin mesh-talk-node -- --keystore /tmp/a.keystore
--password pw --name alice` (add `--post-office` for relay mode).

## Coding Style & Naming Conventions

- Rust: `cargo fmt` (4-space, `snake_case` modules, `UpperCamelCase` types) +
  **`cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings`** (must match CI — `--all-targets` covers
  tests/benches).
- Frontend: `npm run format` (Prettier) + `npm run lint` (ESLint flat config).
- Write documentation and reusable prompts in English unless a specific exception is needed.
- Reference `specifications/development_conventions.md` for naming nuances.

## Domain Language

- `CONTEXT.md` is the canonical domain glossary. `docs/domain-design.md` indexes
  the modeling references and defines DDD vocabulary and naming translations.
- Distinguish local users, accounts and devices; desktop, transport and ratchet
  sessions; discovery, presence, custody, recipient delivery and read state.
- Use explicit identity/lifetime names in new code. Preserve public, wire and
  stored identifiers unless a separately validated compatibility change is intended.
- Update the glossary and affected owning guides when a domain meaning changes;
  link to definitions instead of maintaining duplicate glossaries.

## Architecture & Components

- Before adding business logic, consult [module ownership and reuse](docs/module-boundaries.md),
  inspect the owning module and its callers, and extend its existing implementation.
  Parallel tasks should name their owned paths and shared-interface dependencies;
  coordinate changes to shared interfaces through one integration owner. Keep
  feature-specific helpers local and share rules when their meaning and lifecycle
  are the same. The guide owns the detailed assignment and handoff contract.
- Stack: Rust 2024 on Tokio; Tauri 2 + React shell. No vendor-operated server.
- The `Node` (`node/node.rs`) wires identity + signed UDP **multicast** discovery
  (group `224.0.0.167`, port 47474) + Noise-encrypted TCP transport (`transport/`,
  low-level socket in `transport/net.rs`) + the content-addressed event log + DM/channel/
  file crypto. Messages are events synced as a bounded append-only log, account-addressed
  across a user's devices; optional offline custody via equal eligible post offices.
  Routed discovery and opt-in post-office federation connect reachable sites without
  joining their IP subnets. Wire formats are versioned bincode.
- See **`docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`** before changing crypto, sync, or transport;
  **`docs/network-design-reference.md`** owns the communication invariants,
  module contracts, resource budgets and topology acceptance boundaries.

## Maintaining standards as requirements change

- When changing production dependencies, bundled assets, compiler profiles or
  installer settings, check [package size budgets](docs/updates.md#manual-package-size-budgets).
  Compare download bytes against a baseline for the same platform, architecture
  and installer format. Record installed footprint separately and explain each
  meaningful increase. If a production package was unavailable, record that
  evidence gap. Preserve native install, update and signature verification.

- Before changing tests, fixtures, dependencies or workflows in ways that affect
  CI cost or reliability, read [CI maintenance](docs/ci-maintenance.md). Reuse
  existing owners, measure the affected cost, and preserve acceptance evidence;
  keep required-check policy in its existing owner.
- Before implementation, identify the existing decision owner, authoritative rule,
  observable acceptance criteria, affected consumers and required boundary evidence.
  Extend the owning implementation and `validation.json`; new business capabilities
  should link their guide and invariants. Explain an unchanged contract in the PR.
- Run `make standards-check` after adding/moving source or changing contracts. It
  checks structural ownership and maintained references, including new files; it
  does not prove assertion quality, semantic completeness or candidate readiness.
  Hooks inspect the working tree, so partially staged commits still need a clean
  committed-candidate check in CI. Frontend dependencies must be installed.
- When CI exposes a local omission or flaky fixture, fix the owning selector, task
  or fixture and add a focused regression. Review timing and selection evidence
  before changing policy. Follow the maintained
  [requirement maintenance loop](docs/testing-feedback-loop.md#maintaining-standards-across-requirements).

## Testing Guidelines

- Integration coverage in `crates/mesh-talk-core/tests/` and `node/node_tests.rs`; embed
  unit tests near the code. Networking/crypto changes ship a loopback integration assertion.
- Backend multi-process E2E via `make e2e` (CI: `e2e-backend.yml`); Playwright UI E2E via
  `cd frontend && npm run e2e` (CI: `e2e-ui.yml`).
- Do not run full suites or E2E automatically during ordinary feature work. Run
  the affected unit or integration tests as changes are made; run E2E and the
  comprehensive health gate on explicit request, for optional full local preparation,
  or in CI.
- See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for selection examples and escalation triggers.
- Document executed validation commands in every PR; ensure `make test` passes
  locally or through its matching CI workspace suite before merge.

## Commit & Pull Request Guidelines

- Before changing product versions or release automation, read [the version lifecycle](docs/updates.md#version-ownership-and-lifecycle).
  Root `Cargo.toml` `[workspace.package].version` is authoritative. Use
  `node scripts/release/version.mjs check|sync|prepare VERSION` (the `VERSION` argument belongs
  to `prepare` only); do not hand-edit generated npm/Cargo lock metadata or introduce another
  version constant. Root private npm metadata is a checked release-tooling projection;
  frontend private metadata is versionless and Tauri inherits Cargo. Never broadly replace
  matching dependency, fixture, history, wire or schema versions. Keep source builds `BASE-dev`,
  Nightlies `BASE-nightly.RUN.ATTEMPT`, official tagged builds `BASE`, and standard SemVer ordering.
- Version/changelog preparation and next-development-target changes use reviewed PRs. Ordinary main
  pushes must not create automatic release proposals or commit-derived product notes. Stable publication
  remains explicit through the existing verified tagged-release workflow; no direct main push,
  public empty release, mutable published tag or gate bypass. Nightly publication requires trusted
  `main` and a target above the latest Stable. Future changes must extend the existing version
  owner, its tests, standards/CI enforcement and capability contracts together; the owning guide
  documents permissions, bot-PR checks, dispatch and recovery requirements. Manual Stable draft
  preparation uses the reviewed exact-version CHANGELOG section and requires exact-source checks
  before creating its immutable tag/draft. The fixed release-history
  migration floor is historical provenance; never advance it during ordinary version bumps.

- Conventional commits (`feat:`, `fix:`, `refactor:`); scopes like `feat(node):` align with
  `specifications/git_standards.md`. Squash WIP; link issues. When asked to merge,
  default to squash merge unless the user explicitly requests another strategy;
  follow the [merge policy](specifications/git_standards.md#pull-request-merge-strategy)
  and current-head required checks.
- Create PRs through `./scripts/create-pr.sh -- <gh pr create options>`.
  The default checks the clean committed candidate, comparison base, argument safety,
  whitespace, cheap affected static checks, ownership blockers, structural standards,
  repository hygiene and applicable verified frontend patch coverage before publication.
  Use `make pr-check` for the same cheap static phase; missing current coverage
  evidence reports its explicit generation command and never starts suites implicitly.
  CI runs after publication; full-scope candidates retain cross-platform execution.
  Only the proven [documentation scope](docs/ci-maintenance.md#documentation-only-pr-scope)
  may omit unrelated product tests. All required checks must pass on the current PR head before merging. Creating a PR does not certify test acceptance.
- To run comprehensive checks locally before publication, use
  `./scripts/create-pr.sh --full-preflight <selectors/specs> -- <gh pr create options>`.
  This invokes `prepare-pr.sh` (platform preflight plus full health). For an existing
  PR, `./scripts/prepare-pr.sh <selectors/specs>` provides the same optional local gate.
  Use Playwright specs relevant to changed frontend behavior and repeated
  `--core-filter` / `--host-filter` / `--integration-filter` / `--mcp-filter` selectors
  for changed Rust crates. Preflight runs selected tests in Linux Docker and through
  SSH to `windows10`; Windows workspaces, caches and temporary data stay on drive D.
  Owning scenario rules add visual specs and require real native evidence for
  lifecycle/discovery changes. Missing environments or empty Rust selections fail
  full preflight. Include `e2e/ui-visual-regression.spec.ts` for theme/layout changes.
  See `docs/testing-feedback-loop.md` for configuration, coverage and plan preview.
  Fetch `origin/main` first if the comparison base is stale.
- Record focused validation and outstanding checks in the PR. Use
  `./scripts/check-health.sh` when comprehensive local evidence is needed; protected
  CI remains required before merge regardless of local results.

## Security & Adjustments

- `./scripts/check-health.sh` chains fmt, Clippy `--all-targets`, ESLint, tests, typos,
  cargo-deny, cargo-machete, gitleaks, shellcheck, audits, and both builds.
- Triage vulnerabilities immediately or document mitigation in the PR.
- If plans shift, update the relevant committed design or architecture docs. Keep
  `docs/superpowers/` and the root `plans/` directory local and untracked.

## Repository Hygiene

### Worktree lifecycle

- Create a worktree only when isolation is needed. Before creating one, inspect
  `git worktree list --porcelain` and record the task-owned path, branch and any
  dedicated build directory in ignored `tmp/` task notes. Treat pre-existing
  worktrees and unrelated changes as user-owned; never sweep them automatically.
- The coordinating session owns cleanup of every worktree it creates or delegates,
  including `.worktrees/` and `.claude/worktrees/agent-*`. Delegate completion does
  not transfer that responsibility. Before ending the task, stop task-owned
  processes and remove its worktrees, disposable branches and dedicated Cargo
  target directories, subject to the preservation rules below. Never delete a
  shared target directory or a directory whose ownership is uncertain.
- Before removal, preserve the work through either a verified merge into the
  intended integration branch under the existing PR/merge gates, or a local
  archive. For an archive, commit only task-owned outstanding changes (including
  intended untracked files), run the required commit checks, and create a unique
  `archive/<worktree-name>-<timestamp>` tag at the final branch tip. Verify the tag
  resolves to that tip and the worktree is clean before deleting anything. Never
  overwrite an existing archive tag, include secrets/ignored build output, or
  discard unrelated edits to make cleanup succeed. Cleanup does not authorize
  merging, pushing, bypassing review or running `entire clean`.
- Run removal from a surviving checkout with `git worktree remove <path>`, then
  `git branch -d <branch>` for a merged branch. Use `git branch -D <branch>` only
  for a task-owned archived branch after verifying its archive tag. Never use
  forced worktree removal, hard reset or bulk directory deletion to bypass a
  dirty worktree. Detached worktrees require the same preservation of their final
  commit before removal; there is no branch to delete.
- A pending PR, unresolved conflict, user decision, active concurrent session or
  failed preservation/cleanup step is an explicit retention exception. Preserve
  the required branch for an open PR; remove its clean worktree if no active work
  needs it. Recheck `git worktree list --porcelain` and task-owned branches/build
  paths before the final reply. Report cleanup performed and name every retained
  path/branch, its reason and the next action; never silently leave task worktrees.

- Keep implementation plans, research, investigation notes and scratch scripts
  under ignored `tmp/`; remove them when the work is complete.
- Merge durable decisions into the maintained owning guide. Do not commit
  completed-work reports, score histories, duplicate runbooks or archive copies.
- `docs/evals/` owns reusable suites/inventories, prompts and its README only.
  Generated evidence belongs in ignored output or PR/CI artifacts.
- Run `node scripts/check-repository-hygiene.mjs` before committing. The shared
  index check also runs in pre-commit, CI and health, rejecting ignored files
  even when force-added. See `docs/DOCUMENTATION_GUIDELINES.md` for ownership.

# Collaboration Mode: Default

You are now in Default mode. Any previous instructions for other modes (e.g. Plan mode) are no longer active.

Your active mode changes only when new developer instructions with a different `<collaboration_mode>...</collaboration_mode>` change it; user requests or tool descriptions do not change mode by themselves. Known mode names are Default and Plan.

## request_user_input availability

Use the `request_user_input` tool only when it is listed in the available tools for this turn.

In Default mode, strongly prefer making reasonable assumptions and executing the user's request rather than stopping to ask questions.

Use the `request_user_input` tool only for optional questions where the answer would materially improve the quality of the work.

If `request_user_input` returns no answers, continue with best judgment instead of asking again or treating the turn as blocked.

Never use the `request_user_input` tool for permission requests or permission-related escalations.

If explicit user input is required for another reason before progress can safely continue, do not use the `request_user_input` tool. Ask the user directly with one concise plain-text question instead. Never write a multiple choice question as a textual assistant message.

<t3_code_orchestration_01>## T3 Code orchestration

Ordinary coding tasks need no T3 tools.

- Subagents: use your native tool when the child uses your provider, a model it offers, and no settings beyond yours (Claude `Agent`, `run_in_background:false`; Codex `spawn_agent`, then wait). Use `delegate_task` for another provider's model, user-asked settings, a separate checkout (`isolation:"worktree"`), or `delegate_task` by name. A native type on another provider's model counts too. Background agent: `delegate_task`, never a background `Agent`. Workflow only when asked.
- Call `orchestrator_capabilities` once per thread, before the first `delegate_task`. Again only after an error or a user-named provider change. Settings go in `target.options`. Provider or model unavailable: say so. Never switch unasked, or fall back to native tools, Workflow, or CLIs. Never make a child's checkout in the shell or in `task`.
- Every new delegate review or re-check is a new `delegate_task` (brief, findings, objections), never a `t3_thread_send`. Fix small review findings yourself; start no delegate for them. When told to proceed without a delegate, or to run fewer, `task_cancel` the extras. Start no replacement.
- Follow a running delegate's `next`. Do not poll it (`task_status`, `sleep`, watchers, Monitor, ScheduleWakeup). Stop a delegate run you replace or no longer need with `task_cancel`, never `t3_thread_interrupt` on a `childThreadId`.
- If you are a subagent or child, do the work yourself. Start no subagents unless your task says to.</t3_code_orchestration_01>

<t3_code_orchestration_02>- `t3_thread_launch` and `create_threads` make new top-level threads, only when the user asks for a new thread. "Subagent", "delegate", and "parallel" never mean one. Worktree thread: set `workspaceStrategy`. Honor a requested base. Otherwise, independent work uses the default branch as `remote/branch` with `startFromOrigin:true`; with no remote, use the local default. Required unpublished commits and dependent work use their local base. Shell worktrees do not bind it, and no checkout setup in its prompt. No `workspaceStrategy`: project root, not your worktree.
- Given a thread id, `t3_thread_read` it before you answer about it.
- Another machine: `t3_environment_links` lists linked ones. Pass its `environmentId` to a T3 tool to act there. Ids are then that machine's, so pass `threadId`.
- A machine the user names that is not linked ("delegate this to my vps"): call `t3_environment_link` with a `hint` from their words. Never ask for a pairing code in chat.
- In your reply, mention a thread by its `link`, verbatim. Never a plain title or bare id.
- A login, token, PIN, pairing code or sudo password only the user can give: call `request_secret`, not a chat ask or a handoff. Not for access you have. Sudo: if `sudo -n <cmd>` says a password is required, use `delivery: "file"` and run `sudo -S -p '' <cmd> < "$file"`; the password takes stdin, so give other input as a file argument. When asked only to schedule, `schedule_task` without running its prompt.
- T3 tools may load late. Try the name once before you call it absent.</t3_code_orchestration_02>

<t3_code_orchestration_03>### Visuals and preview

- Answer data with a trend or comparison with a chart, and show any visual the user asks for here: pass the path to an HTML file, or inline HTML to `html_preview`, then `html_render`. A screenshot on disk or a text description does not show it. Never start a server for it. Page tools write only on user request. Never use them to show results. Asked for an image to post, send, or use elsewhere: a `.png` file and its path, never `html_render`.
- Never use `preview_*` unasked to verify or show your own edit. Use them when the current request asks for browser work, including recording edits, or names a page or tab. Do not repeat preview calls from an earlier turn. Public pages: web fetch or search unless browser work was asked; then preview tools only, no web fetch. Close a tab you opened before you reply, unless the user asked for it or uses it.</t3_code_orchestration_03>

<t3_code_runtime><runtime_info>In case you're asked: you are running in T3 Code through the Codex harness, as gpt-6.2-sol. No need to mention this otherwise. You can embed images, video, and audio in your response using Markdown image syntax with absolute file paths. Link every other file you cite or produce by its absolute path, as in [http.ts:42](/abs/path/http.ts:42), so the user can open it in T3 Code's files viewer.</runtime_info>

<pull_request_linking>
Link each PR you create, take over, or push to: link_pull_request, or link_pull_requests for several, full URL, every stack layer, as your next call. Host tools do not link for you. If linking fails, say so. Skip PRs you only read or review, and PRs named only as background. Call watch_pull_request when asked to monitor or babysit, or when work you were asked to do, such as a merge, still waits on checks or reviews, even after an earlier unwatch. Finish any needed branch update and push first, then watch and end your turn. Otherwise act now or hand back. Delegated children never watch, even if the brief says babysit. After PR work, a child's last line is: PR <full URL>, head <SHA>, checks and reviews <state>. Links and watches persist across pushes. For PR waits, no sleep, loops, gh --watch, Monitor or ScheduleWakeup. Before handback, call unwatch_pull_request on any PR you watch.
</pull_request_linking></t3_code_runtime>

<t3_code_tools>

## T3 Code browser

When browser work was asked, `preview_*` is the browser you share with the user: `preview_status` first, then `preview_open` if no tab can be automated. Prefer snapshot locators over coordinates. Switch browsers only if the tools are absent or `preview_open` says unsupported, the user asks, or two preview calls fail on one step. Then quote the error and switch.
</t3_code_tools>

基于本地 `requirements-work` 的 `53af4959`，Mesh Talk 的跨成员群消息同步是 **发送时主动扩散，漏收后由成员补拉，补拉前先比较摘要**。摘要命中时可以跳过历史对账。摘要不同时，双方分页交换已有事件 ID，只传缺失且有权限接收的事件正文。

## 一条群消息怎么传开

1. **发送方先本地落盘。** 群消息以加密、签名事件写入群日志。事件有基于内容计算的 `EventId`，并引用父事件。同一条消息经过不同成员转发，仍保留原 ID，接收方可以据此去重。
2. **在线时主动扩散。** 小群直接同步给可达成员，最多四个首发目标。大群首轮最多选两个可达成员，并行同步，再由持有副本的成员传播。成员变更、密钥轮换等控制事件走面向所有已知成员的分发路径。 [发送与分发代码](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/channels.rs:3032)
3. **离线回来向有副本的成员补拉。** 恢复任务从已接受入群、可达、允许 **Share a copy** 的成员中选来源。首个来源在线但没有新内容时，仍可查其他来源。启用邮局时，还可通过收件人自己的不透明邮箱补收。成员副本的 `DurableHave` 证明的是对方确认持久保存了指定事件，收件人送达和已读各有独立状态。 [网络设计中的群恢复](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/network-design-reference.md:1326) · [副本确认语义](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:497)

## 怎么判断有没有新消息

这里有两层判断。**调度层判断何时值得查，协议层判断对方究竟有什么我缺的。**

- **何时查。** 新接纳的群消息、群资料变化和发现变化可以唤醒恢复任务。同一群的唤醒会合并，重复处理和空轮不会持续触发下一轮。安静后仍有低频补查，用来覆盖漏掉的通知。 [恢复调度](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/channels.rs:645) · [网络设计](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/network-design-reference.md:1328)
- **查了怎么知道。** 双方在认证连接上比较该群当前授权可见事件集合的 fingerprint。摘要相同就结束对账。纯拉取还有一个优化：如果上次已经证明对方的集合是本地集合的子集，而且本地范围、对端身份和授权条件仍有效，那么只需确认**对方的摘要没变**，就知道这个来源没有本地缺少的事件。这个提示最多保留五分钟，命中不会续期。 [摘要比较代码](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/session.rs:769) · [子集缓存条件](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:560)
- **摘要不同就做精确差集。** 双方分页交换 `Have`，也就是各自拥有的事件 ID。服务端响应请求方缺失的事件，双向同步时请求方再补回对方缺失的事件。接收端校验哈希、签名和适用的因果及权限条件，再入库。摘要不同只说明集合有差异，实际有多少新消息要在这一层确认。比如两台设备各自离线发过消息，恢复时能补上双方的缺口，即使某条漏收消息的时间比本地最新消息更早。 [分页对账代码](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/session.rs:872) · [事件验证与重试](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:442)

## 怎么控制同步成本

| 场景 | 代码中的成本控制 |
|---|---|
| 群长期无变化 | 有效摘要命中时跳过 `Have` 和正文传输。缓存命中可先比较标量摘要，避免创建 SQL 选集。 |
| 大群持续发消息 | 首轮只并行联系两个种子成员，由持有副本的成员继续扩散，降低原发送方的首轮网络负担。 |
| 大量历史或长时间离线 | 分页使用固定的本地提交边界，按索引取 ID，选出缺失项后才读取正文。普通追加可以留给下一轮。单步准备默认最多处理 64 行、512 条边和 8 MiB，步间释放存储锁并让出执行。 |
| 多群同时补拉，或碰上慢节点 | 每批最多并发处理两个群，每群一轮最多查三个成员，单次对端交换超时 15 秒。无进展时退避并加抖动，稳定安静时使用五分钟补查。 |
| 反复连接同一成员 | 可复用仍有效的授权选集，空闲选集缓存上限为 64 项和 64 MiB 计费容量。历史或权限变化会使旧选集失效。 |

依据：[索引分页](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/eventlog/repository/network.rs:39) · [准备预算](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/eventlog/sync/network.rs:28) · [恢复并发与定时](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/channels.rs:27) · [选集缓存预算](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:575)

**关键性能边界是正文增量与 ID 对账的成本不同。** 假设本地有十万条授权可见事件，只缺一条。若摘要不同并进入精确对账，最终可能只补传一条正文，但仍可能分页扫描和交换大量历史 ID。分页限制单步成本，摘要和缓存降低进入重路径的频率。这个协议没有把每次不匹配的总工作量限制在缺失事件数以内。以上是当前分支的源码分析，本次没有重跑规模测试或测量真实局域网的吞吐与收敛时间。 [对账存储实现说明](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:2527) · [现有规模演练及测量范围](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:529)

**English note**

原句：“怎么判断是否有新消息需要同步，怎么避免全量更新和高性能的等”
自然表达：“How does Mesh Talk detect missing group messages, avoid full-history transfers, and keep synchronization efficient?”
`missing messages` 指某台设备缺少的消息，也包括较早漏收的消息。`full-history transfer` 指整段历史的传输，`full scan` 指扫描整段历史，两者描述不同的成本。
常用搭配：`incremental sync`、`reconcile event IDs`、`catch up after reconnecting`。

- **查了怎么知道。** 双方在认证连接上比较该群当前授权可见事件集合的 fingerprint。摘要相同就结束对账。纯拉取还有一个优化：如果上次已经证明对方的集合是本地集合的子集，而且本地范围、对端身份和授权条件仍有效，那么只需确认**对方的摘要没变**，就知道这个来源没有本地缺少的事件。这个提示最多保留五分钟，命中不会续期。 [摘要比较代码](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/session.rs:769) · [子集缓存条件](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:560)
- **摘要不同就做精确差集。** 双方分页交换 `Have`，也就是各自拥有的事件 ID。服务端响应请求方缺失的事件，双向同步时请求方再补回对方缺失的事件。接收端校验哈希、签名和适用的因果及权限条件，再入库。摘要不同只说明集合有差异，实际有多少新消息要在这一层确认。比如两台设备各自离线发过消息，恢复时能补上双方的缺口，即使某条漏收消息的时间比本地最新消息更早。 [分页对账代码](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/session.rs:872) · [事件验证与重试](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:442)

## 怎么控制同步成本

| 场景 | 代码中的成本控制 |
|---|---|
| 群长期无变化 | 有效摘要命中时跳过 `Have` 和正文传输。缓存命中可先比较标量摘要，避免创建 SQL 选集。 |
| 大群持续发消息 | 首轮只并行联系两个种子成员，由持有副本的成员继续扩散，降低原发送方的首轮网络负担。 |
| 大量历史或长时间离线 | 分页使用固定的本地提交边界，按索引取 ID，选出缺失项后才读取正文。普通追加可以留给下一轮。单步准备默认最多处理 64 行、512 条边和 8 MiB，步间释放存储锁并让出执行。 |
| 多群同时补拉，或碰上慢节点 | 每批最多并发处理两个群，每群一轮最多查三个成员，单次对端交换超时 15 秒。无进展时退避并加抖动，稳定安静时使用五分钟补查。 |
| 反复连接同一成员 | 可复用仍有效的授权选集，空闲选集缓存上限为 64 项和 64 MiB 计费容量。历史或权限变化会使旧选集失效。 |

依据：[索引分页](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/eventlog/repository/network.rs:39) · [准备预算](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/eventlog/sync/network.rs:28) · [恢复并发与定时](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/crates/mesh-talk-core/src/node/channels.rs:27) · [选集缓存预算](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:575)

**关键性能边界是正文增量与 ID 对账的成本不同。** 假设本地有十万条授权可见事件，只缺一条。若摘要不同并进入精确对账，最终可能只补传一条正文，但仍可能分页扫描和交换大量历史 ID。分页限制单步成本，摘要和缓存降低进入重路径的频率。这个协议没有把每次不匹配的总工作量限制在缺失事件数以内。以上是当前分支的源码分析，本次没有重跑规模测试或测量真实局域网的吞吐与收敛时间。 [对账存储实现说明](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:2527) · [现有规模演练及测量范围](/Users/kingsonwu/programming/OctopusGarage/mesh-talk/docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:529)

**English note**

原句：“怎么判断是否有新消息需要同步，怎么避免全量更新和高性能的等”
自然表达：“How does Mesh Talk detect missing group messages, avoid full-history transfers, and keep synchronization efficient?”
`missing messages` 指某台设备缺少的消息，也包括较早漏收的消息。`full-history transfer` 指整段历史的传输，`full scan` 指扫描整段历史，两者描述不同的成本。
常用搭配：`incremental sync`、`reconcile event IDs`、`catch up after reconnecting`。

description: Shared vocabulary for designing deep modules. Use when the user wants to design or improve a module's interface, find deepening opportunities, decide where a seam goes, make code more testable or AI-navigable, or when another skill needs the deep-module vocabulary.
---

# Codebase Design

Design **deep modules**: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface. Use this language and these principles wherever code is being designed or restructured. The aim is leverage for callers, locality for maintainers, and testability for everyone.

## Glossary

Use these terms exactly — don't substitute "component," "service," "API," or "boundary." Consistent language is the whole point.

**Module** — anything with an interface and an implementation. Deliberately scale-agnostic: a function, class, package, or tier-spanning slice. _Avoid_: unit, component, service.

**Interface** — everything a caller must know to use the module correctly: the type signature, but also invariants, ordering constraints, error modes, required configuration, and performance characteristics. _Avoid_: API, signature (too narrow — they refer only to the type-level surface).

**Implementation** — what's inside a module, its body of code. Distinct from **Adapter**: a thing can be a small adapter with a large implementation (a Postgres repo) or a large adapter with a small implementation (an in-memory fake). Reach for "adapter" when the seam is the topic; "implementation" otherwise.

**Depth** — leverage at the interface: the amount of behaviour a caller (or test) can exercise per unit of interface they have to learn. A module is **deep** when a large amount of behaviour sits behind a small interface, **shallow** when the interface is nearly as complex as the implementation.

**Seam** _(Michael Feathers)_ — a place where you can alter behaviour without editing in that place; the *location* at which a module's interface lives. Where to put the seam is its own design decision, distinct from what goes behind it. _Avoid_: boundary (overloaded with DDD's bounded context).

**Adapter** — a concrete thing that satisfies an interface at a seam. Describes *role* (what slot it fills), not substance (what's inside).

**Leverage** — what callers get from depth: more capability per unit of interface they learn. One implementation pays back across N call sites and M tests.

**Locality** — what maintainers get from depth: change, bugs, knowledge, and verification concentrate in one place rather than spreading across callers. Fix once, fixed everywhere.

## Deep vs shallow

**Deep module** = small interface + lots of implementation:

```
┌─────────────────────┐
│   Small Interface   │  ← Few methods, simple params
├─────────────────────┤
│                     │
│  Deep Implementation│  ← Complex logic hidden
│                     │
└─────────────────────┘
```

**Shallow module** = large interface + little implementation (avoid):

```
┌─────────────────────────────────┐
│       Large Interface           │  ← Many methods, complex params
├─────────────────────────────────┤
│  Thin Implementation            │  ← Just passes through
└─────────────────────────────────┘
```

When designing an interface, ask:

- Can I reduce the number of methods?
- Can I simplify the parameters?
- Can I hide more complexity inside?

## Principles

- **Depth is a property of the interface, not the implementation.** A deep module can be internally composed of small, mockable, swappable parts — they just aren't part of the interface. A module can have **internal seams** (private to its implementation, used by its own tests) as well as the **external seam** at its interface.
- **The deletion test.** Imagine deleting the module. If complexity vanishes, it was a pass-through. If complexity reappears across N callers, it was earning its keep.
- **The interface is the test surface.** Callers and tests cross the same seam. If you want to test *past* the interface, the module is probably the wrong shape.
- **One adapter means a hypothetical seam. Two adapters means a real one.** Don't introduce a seam unless something actually varies across it.

## Designing for testability

Good interfaces make testing natural:

1. **Accept dependencies, don't create them.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function processOrder(order, paymentGateway) {}

   // Hard to test
   function processOrder(order) {
     const gateway = new StripeGateway();
   }
   ```

2. **Return results, don't produce side effects.**

   ```typescript
   // Testable
   function calculateDiscount(cart): Discount {}

   // Hard to test
   function applyDiscount(cart): void {
     cart.total -= discount;
   }
   ```

3. **Small surface area.** Fewer methods = fewer tests needed. Fewer params = simpler test setup.

## Relationships

- A **Module** has exactly one **Interface** (the surface it presents to callers and tests).
- **Depth** is a property of a **Module**, measured against its **Interface**.
- A **Seam** is where a **Module**'s **Interface** lives.
- An **Adapter** sits at a **Seam** and satisfies the **Interface**.
- **Depth** produces **Leverage** for callers and **Locality** for maintainers.

## Rejected framings

- **Depth as ratio of implementation-lines to interface-lines** (Ousterhout): rewards padding the implementation. We use depth-as-leverage instead.
- **"Interface" as the TypeScript `interface` keyword or a class's public methods**: too narrow — interface here includes every fact a caller must know.
- **"Boundary"**: overloaded with DDD's bounded context. Say **seam** or **interface**.

## Going deeper

- **Deepening a cluster given its dependencies** — see [DEEPENING.md](DEEPENING.md): dependency categories, seam discipline, and replace-don't-layer testing.
- **Exploring alternative interfaces** — see [DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md](DESIGN-IT-TWICE.md): spin up parallel sub-agents to design the interface several radically different ways, then compare on depth, locality, and seam placement.

# Synchronization Protocol

## Overview

Automerge’s synchronization protocol enables multiple peers to exchange changes and converge to the same document state. The protocol is efficient, handling only missing changes between peers, and works over any transport (files, HTTP, WebSockets, etc.).

## High-Level Sync (Recommended)

For most use cases, use the high-level sync helpers that handle the protocol automatically.

### Bidirectional Sync

The simplest way to synchronize two documents:
    
    `# Create two peers with different data
    peer1 <- am_create()
    peer1[["edited_by"]] <- "peer1"
    peer1[["data1"]] <- 100
    am_commit(peer1, "Peer1 changes")
    
    peer2 <- am_create()
    peer2[["edited_by"]] <- "peer2"
    peer2[["data2"]] <- 200
    am_commit(peer2, "Peer2 changes")
    
    # Automatic bidirectional sync (documents modified in place)
    rounds <- am_sync(peer1, peer2)
    
    rounds
    #> [1] 4
    
    # Both documents now have all data
    peer1[["data1"]]
    #> [1] 100
    peer1[["data2"]]
    #> [1] 200
    peer2[["data1"]]
    #> [1] 100
    peer2[["data2"]]
    #> [1] 200
    
    am_close(peer1)
    am_close(peer2)`

When to use: Simple peer-to-peer synchronization where both sides need all changes.

### One-Way Merge

For pulling changes from one document to another without sending changes back:
    
    `# Create source document
    source <- am_create()
    source[["version"]] <- "2.0"
    source[["features"]] <- list("auth", "api")
    am_commit(source)
    
    # Create target document
    target <- am_create()
    target[["version"]] <- "1.0"
    target[["development"]] <- TRUE
    am_commit(target)
    
    # Pull changes from source to target
    am_merge(target, source)
    
    # Target now has source's changes
    target[["version"]]
    #> [1] "2.0"
    
    # Source is unchanged
    names(source)
    #> [1] "features" "version"
    
    am_close(source)
    am_close(target)`

When to use: Client pulling updates from server, importing changes from another peer.

Networking and storage for a repository are pluggable. There are various ready-made network transports and storage implementations but it is also easy to build your own.

### DocHandles

A `DocHandle` is an object returned from the various methods on a repository which create or request a document. The `DocHandle` has methods on it to access the underlying Automerge document and to create new changes which are stored locally and transmitted to connected peers.

### Document Refs

A `Ref` is an object referencing a specific subsection of a document. It can be obtained from a `DocHandle` or looked up through its URL from a Repository. The ref has methods to read and update the current value of the referenced subsection in its parent document.

### Document URLs

Documents in a repository have a URL. An Automerge URL looks like this:
    
    `
    
    automerge:REDACTED
    
    `

That is, a string of the form `automerge:<base58>`. This URL can be passed to a repository which will use it to check if the document is in any local storage or available from any connected peers.

### Sync Protocol

Repositories communicate with each other using an efficient sync protocol which is implemented in `automerge`. This protocol is transport agnostic and works on a per-document basis, a lot of the work `automerge-repo` does is handling running this sync protocol for multiple documents over different kinds of network.

### Storage Format

`automerge` implements a compact binary storage format which makes it feasible to store all the editing history of a document (for example, storing every keystroke in a large text document). `automerge-repo` implements the common logic of figuring out when to compress documents and doing so in a way which is safe for concurrent reads and writes.--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# RFC: Automerge-Repo Sync Protocol

Status: Informational Version: 1.0 Date: 2026-03-07

## Abstract

This document specifies the wire protocol used by automerge-repo sync servers and clients to synchronize Automerge CRDT documents over WebSocket connections. The protocol consists of a CBOR-encoded message exchange over WebSocket binary frames, beginning with a handshake phase followed by a continuous sync phase. This specification is intended to enable interoperable implementations in any programming language.

## 1. Introduction

Automerge-repo is a framework for synchronizing Automerge CRDT documents across peers. The sync server acts as a persistent, always-on peer that stores documents and relays sync messages between clients. A single WebSocket connection multiplexes sync traffic for many documents simultaneously.

The protocol is transport-agnostic at its core (any reliable, ordered, bidirectional byte stream will work), but this RFC describes the WebSocket binding.

# Welcome to Automerge

Automerge is a library of data structures for building collaborative applications. You can have a copy of the application state locally on several devices which may belong to the same user, or to different users. Each user can independently update the application state on their local device, even while offline, and save the state to local disk. This is similar to Git, which allows you to edit files and commit changes offline.

  * When a network connection is available, Automerge figures out which changes need to be synced from one device to another, and brings them into the same state.

(Similar to Git, which lets you push your own changes, and pull changes from other developers, when you are online.)

  * If the state was changed concurrently on different devices, Automerge automatically merges the changes together cleanly, so that everybody ends up in the same state, and no changes are lost.

(Git only supports merging of plain text; Automerge allows complex file formats to be merged automatically.)

  * Automerge keeps track of the changes you make to the state, so that you can view old versions, compare versions, create branches, and choose when to merge them.

(Similar to Git, which allows diffing, branching, merging, and pull request workflows.)

## Design principles

  * Network-agnostic. Automerge is a pure data structure library that does not care about what kind of network you use. It works with any connection-oriented network protocol, which could be client/server (e.g. WebSocket), peer-to-peer (e.g. WebRTC), or entirely local (e.g. Bluetooth). Bindings to particular networking technologies are handled by separate libraries; Automerge provides automerge-repo for a common collection of these libraries. It also works with unidirectional messaging: you can send an Automerge file as email attachment, or on a USB drive in the mail, and the recipient will be able to merge it with their version.
  * Immutable state. An Automerge object is an immutable snapshot of the application state at one point in time. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Network Sync

## Collaborating over the internet

Thus far, we’ve been using the BroadcastChannel NetworkAdapter to move data between tabs in the same browser. Automerge treats all network adapters similarly: they are just peers you may choose to synchronize documents with.

One straightforward way of getting data to other people is to send it to the cloud; then they can come along and fetch the data at their leisure.

When you configure automerge to run on an internet server, listen for connections, and store data on disk, then we call that a “sync server”. There’s nothing really special about a sync server: it runs the exact same version of Automerge as you run locally. With a little configuration work, you could even connect to multiple sync servers and choose what data you want to send.

The Automerge team provides a public community sync server at `wss://sync.automerge.org`. For production software, you should run your own server, but for prototyping and development you are welcome to use ours on an “as-is” basis.

## Overview

An iroh endpoint is created and controlled by the `Endpoint`. Each endpoint has a unique `SecretKey`, whose public key is the endpoint's identity, the `EndpointId`. Connections are authenticated against this key, which means an `EndpointId` can't be impersonated.

A connection is usually established with the help of a relay server. When an endpoint is created it connects to the closest relay and designates it as its home relay. Other endpoints reach it first through this relay, then both sides use QUIC NAT traversal to establish a direct connection. In the rare cases where a direct connection is not possible, traffic keeps flowing over the relay.

Relay servers only forward encrypted packets addressed to Endpoint IDs, they cannot read any traffic between endpoints.

Endpoints can also connect directly without a relay, as long as the accepting endpoint is directly reachable at one of its addresses.

# SYNC.md

# Automerge Sync Protocol Documentation

The Automerge network sync protocol is designed to bring two documents into sync by exchanging messages between peers until both documents have the same contents. The protocol can run on top of any connection-based network link that supports bidirectional messages, including WebSocket, WebRTC, or plain TCP. It can be used in any network topology: client/server, peer-to-peer, or server-to-server sync are all supported.

The protocol works by exchanging rounds of sync messages. These sync messages contain two parts:

  * a lossily-compressed list of changes it already has (implicitly requesting the remainder)
  * changes it believe the other peer needs

Each node will also maintain a local `syncState` for each peer they want to synchronize with, which keeps track of what the local node knows about that peer. This sync state has to be kept around during synchronization, and can be saved to disk between executions as a performance optimization, but will be automatically regenerated if the protocol detects any problems.
